utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I see that the appearances of the parties are, as far as lead counsel are concerned, the same as yesterday. I will not repeat it at every hearing. We have a few matters to deal with before the Chamber invites the Prosecution to call its first witness. I have on my agenda, first of all, that the Defence may respond to two motions we discussed recently. That should be done in private session. There is another matter with which I could start right away, and that is instructions concerning the Rule 92 bis motion of the 19th of February, 2007, Mr. Re. The instructions concern the Rule 92 bis motion of the 19th of February, and the Defence, all Defence teams, have now responded to this motion. Before proceeding to take a decision on the motion, the Trial Chamber wishes to bring to the Prosecution's attention that there are certain discrepancies between the motion and the witness list which was filed last Friday. There are, for example, certain witnesses who, according to the motion, will be called to give some evidence viva voce in addition to the evidence which the Prosecution seeks to introduce under Rule 92 bis. In the witness list, however, no time is allocated for examination-in-chief for these witnesses. Therefore, the Trial Chamber asks the Prosecution to compare the motion of 19 February 2007 with the witness list filed on 2 March 2007, and to file a corrected Rule 92 bis motion, or at least a correction to that motion. The Defence will then be provided with an opportunity to amend their responses to the Rule 92 bis motion, should this be necessary. This concludes the Trial Chamber's instructions relating to the Rule 92 bis motion of the 19th of February, 2007. Another matter which I'd like to clarify, first of all. Mr. Re, the next witness, not a witness to be called today, but the witness next to that, would that be a witness which bears the pseudonym W38? W, of course, stands for witness, witness 38. Would that be correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We also understand you'll seek protective measures for that witness. Any idea on when you'll file an application for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was being drafted this morning. It should be filed fairly soon, I would hope. I will have a look at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Having clarified this, I would have in mind to give an oral decision on the -- and I think we can do that in open session, on the "Confidential Application on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj to Exclude Testimony pursuant to Rule 89(D)" in respect of the next witness to come. At the same time, I am informed that there are even other submissions to be made in respect to the testimony of that witness. If that would be the case, then we'll first hear that and then see whether we still could deliver the decision we have reached at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are no additional oral submissions. I was asked to identify what issues there were to be dealt with this morning -- or this afternoon, before the witness was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it was simply in respect of the fact that there's an issue outstanding or a motion outstanding that requires to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I might, Your Honours, I don't know if it's necessary, but just to make sure the record is clear. We do join the submission made with regard to the issues raised in this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean that's the 89(D) motion filed on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- I'll then deliver the decision. That's an oral decision on the motion of the 5th of March, filed on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj, but now joined by all Defence counsel, or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: By all Defence counsel, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By all defence counsel. So all three accused, that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We will always take care to notify the court, if for any reason we don't join in any motion, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I think we'd prefer -- a brief yes would do, but to work on the basis of what has not been said is a little bit risky. So if you'd say, "We join," that will be enough. It will be your words, so for the -- on behalf of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision is regarding, and now I'll give the title of the motion, the "Confidential Application on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj to Exclude Testimony pursuant to Rule 89(D)," which was filed on the 5th of March, 2007. In its application, the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj seeks to, and I quote, "exclude the testimonies, or portions thereof, of SST7/28 and Marijana Andjelkovic, who are scheduled to be called as the Prosecution's first two witnesses." The Prosecution has not responded to the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, the Prosecution hasn't. We received it yesterday, and I understood there would have been oral argument from the Prosecution, if necessary, rather than a written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, we discussed -- the position of the Prosecution became clear from the attached correspondence. I think that's when I referred to that yesterday. If that would not be your position, then, of course, I would give you an opportunity and I'll immediately stop delivering the decision. But if your position is reflected properly in the correspondence, then, of course, we have looked at that when considering the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was certainly our preliminary view in relation to the evidence I propose to adduce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to add anything, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Only if it would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber in reaching its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you want to respond, you may respond. However, if you do not respond and if I would continue to deliver the decision, then it would result in a denial of the motion. So I don't know whether it's still of any use for you to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then I'll continue to deliver that decision. The last line I read before was that the Prosecution has not responded to the application, and that still is now the case. We have in the meantime been informed that the testimony of witness 28 will be postponed. The Chamber will deal with the part of the Defence application pertaining to witness 28 in due course, and, of course, if there would be any reason for you to further respond in relation to witness 28, you would have an opportunity to do so, Mr. Re. In relation to the evidence to be given by Witness Andjelkovic, the Chamber will deal with this part of the application now, considering that her testimony is imminent. The Defence seeks exclusion of potential allegations which have not yet been and are not being tendered into evidence by any party at this stage of the proceedings. Therefore, the Chamber considers the Defence application premature and therefore rejects it. Nevertheless, the Chamber wishes to notify the parties of some general guidelines to be adhered to when eliciting evidence from witnesses. As a general rule, opinion evidence should not be elicited from fact witnesses. Inviting the witness to speculate should also be avoided. In cases in which it is not clear what the factual basis is of a witness's testimony, the parties are required to explore the basis of the witness's knowledge in relation to his or her testimony. As to second-degree hearsay evidence, or hearsay that is even more remote than that, such evidence as a rule does not assist the Chamber and the parties are urged to avoid it as much as possible, keeping in mind that transparency in the flow of information is of greatest importance in relation to such evidence. This concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. Then we'll turn into private session to give an opportunity to the Defence to respond to the two motions, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready, Mr. Re, to call its first witness, which I understand is a witness for whom no protective measures are needed, and the witness being Marijana Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct. It's Marijana Andjelkovic, the first witness. No protective measures are required. She's outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam. I understand that you're Marijana Andjelkovic. Before you give evidence before this Chamber, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed down to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Ms. Andjelkovic. You'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Once he has finished his examination, you, although most likely not today, will be cross-examined then by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your name is Marijana Andjelkovic -- I understand you're testifying in English, if we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Marijana Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you're testifying in English?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were born in 1963?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I currently work at the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you do there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I am the chief editor. I have a title of human rights officer, but I mainly edit and prepare for publishing the reports that are compiled by the human rights department of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to get a little bit of background to let the Trial Chamber know who you are and where you're coming from and the experience you had in 1998, in testifying as to the matters relevant to the court. Can you tell the Court what you were doing -- your employment in the 1990s leading up to 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In the -- I first went to Kosovo in 1994. I was working for about 18 months for an NGO called Doctors of the World USA. I was working on a -- it was mainly a TV-controlled programme. Then I was -- I went to England for a while, and then when I came back, I was working for another NGO, another US NGO, International Orthodox Christian Charities. This was mainly on refugee assistance programmes. I was dividing my time between Kosovo and -- and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Orthodox Christian Charities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you finish working there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In early December 1997, and then I started to work for the Humanitarian Law Centre in January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just pause -- ask you to pause there. What is the Humanitarian Law Centre?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Centre is an NGO that was set up, I think, in 1992, and what it was doing in both Bosnia and later on in Kosovo, it was following the conflict and interviewing witnesses or victims of humanitarian law violations, people who had been exposed, civilians predominantly, who have been exposed to violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is that an organisation associated with the Natasa Kandic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Natasa is an executive director and a founder of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And does it have any party line? Is it affiliated with any political organisation or political state or political entity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge, it isn't. It was purely there because it was necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, something happened with your microphone, so we are not -- it may be that you've touched the button. I'm not quite sure. The button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I'm afraid I pushed, by mistake, the priority button. I apologise. It's always good to first try to find the fault with yourself and only then to look at others. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was asking you a moment ago about the political affiliations, if any, of the Humanitarian Law Centre.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I would say -- I would say not. Natasa Kandic is probably one of the strongest campaigners for human rights and also for the prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you say "prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia," are you referring to any particular side to any of the conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Not really, not really. The Humanitarian Law Centre was working with all civilians, it didn't have any preferences. Although I have to say, and one may see that from public statements of the organisation, that they would like to focus on Serbia and they do focus on Serbia, but it's because they are registered in Belgrade, and one should clean one's own yard first, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go back to Kosovo in late 1997 and early 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did the HLC, short for Humanitarian Law Centre, have its offices?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It had offices in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And also in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Also in Belgrade, yes. It is based in Belgrade, but it had a small office in Pristina, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And why did it have an office in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I only started to work in January 1998, but it is my understanding that there has -- there had already been a person working in Pristina, and she was interviewing people who were exposed to police harassment at the time, whether it was -- sometimes it was weapons search; sometimes people would get arrested; and sometimes people were mistreated by police. There were different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "police harassment," are you referring to the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the job that you got with the Humanitarian Law Centre in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In 1998, I have been asked to -- to start working on what was then called ethnic minorities issues, but then what happened is that a conflict started in Kosovo, so that took -- took up most of my time. So I went more to Kosovo then -- then I had time to -- to do other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, why did you go to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just in general terms. I'll get more specific in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah. Sometime in February, there were reports in the press that there were attacks on ethnic Serb houses in more remote areas, in more remote villages, in Kosovo. So Natasa thought that it would not be a bad idea to go to Kosovo and try to get in touch with people and see if there -- if there was any truth in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in case it's not quite clear for the Chamber, what was the job? Can you describe, as precisely as possible, the job that Natasa Kandic asked you to do.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. I was supposed to get in touch, try to visit these villages that were mentioned in reports, and I was supposed to find these families and talk to them, and see if they'd really been attacked or not, and then take their statement -- "statement" is maybe too strong a word. But just ask them what had happened and what they'd noticed. And then I was supposed to put it in a report, of a form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a job description?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't really remember. I think there must have been something, because I did have an interview. But it was -- it was a temporary placement, as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, go to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1998, how many times, approximately, did you go to Kosovo, and for what -- for what period?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Up until the end of September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Gosh, it must have been 18 times. More than a dozen. I would spend -- I would go down there at least once every ten days and spend anything from two or three days to -- to a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you went there, did you go alone or with other people?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I would mostly, because I would go there from Belgrade, I would mostly travel alone, although there were cases when I would travel with some other colleagues. But the first time I went -- the first time I went, I wasn't actually alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your methodology, about what you did when you actually went there. You tell -- can you tell the Trial Chamber about the first time you went to Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and what you did and how you did things.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. Well, it was a fairly simple methodology. You have to understand this is a non-governmental organisation. And what we would do is we would talk to people who were either victims or witnesses of things that happened, and we would talk to them, we would write that down and then put it in a form. And then HLC had lawyers as well, and they would look through it and see whether there were any violations and what violations that would be. And then we'd -- also, they'd give us guidance as to what to look for --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: -- specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you would write it down, are you referring to a notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you keep -- did you keep notes or take notes --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- of your interviews with the people you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you took the notes, what did you do with the contents of your notebook afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. Well, I've collected a few of these very cheap but practical noteblocks, and I can't recall exactly now. I know who I gave them to, but I can't remember when. It may have been before the bombing. Of this, I'm not quite sure. But I gave them to a colleague that I worked with in the Kosovo Verification Mission, who was an OSCE. She was my immediate supervisor when I was with the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not framing my questions clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm actually directing you to is, after you had recorded your observations or conversations --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- in a notebook, what did you do then? What was the process or methodology of the HLC?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right, sorry. What I would then do is I would type them in a computer, in a document. There was a form that we had with certain details, and then we would type that in. We would type every incident into one of these forms and file it. And I would do that either in Pristina, in the office, or I would go -- whenever I was in Belgrade, I would collect quite a few of these incidents and then type them all at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Tell the Trial Chamber about the form. What was actually on the form?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The form was fairly simple. It had, you know, the name of the victim, the name of the witness or the person that we talked to. It had the date of the incident, it had the location, and it had this one section that was violations. But this was actually not really filled by us, unless it was obvious; for example, if somebody went missing so that would be obvious. Everything else was done by the -- with the file once the lawyer got that; and then we would -- the main thing for us would be the incident, how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. You said you typed it. Do you mean into a computer?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. [B/C/S on English channel

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There must be a mistake in switching. We just received B/C/S on the channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, there has been, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you please repeat your last question so that the witness can answer it, your last question being: "You said you typed it. Do you mean into a computer?" And then could you please respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You typed it into a computer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I typed it into a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what happened to the information you typed into a computer. You mentioned some reports a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. What would happen then is all these files were kept at the HLC, and then occasionally there would be a public statement or there would be a public report that was based on the interviews that we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any of the information, which you took from witnesses or people you spoke to on the ground, make it into these published reports?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- there was -- one of the reports that I remember was reports -- a report about the missing people in Kosovo, and I think that was in June 1998 that was published. There's a little brochure. They were called spot reports, if I remember -- spotlight reports, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go the first time you went to Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The first time I went to Kosovo, I first went to -- to Drenica. But that was quite disorganised, and I didn't have a report from there. That was after the first major incident. But then immediately after that, I went west and I went to Pec and Decane, in that area, because there were reports that people's houses, most of all, were attacked in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when was it that you first went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Oh, I first went on the 20 -- I arrived on the 28th of February, and then it was the beginning of March, maybe the 1st, 2nd, of March, so the first week of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Court, the Trial Chamber, about what you observed when you went to Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Oh, that was -- that was actually quite strange, because I went with another -- with two colleagues; one of whom was not even working in the field, but he was driving the car. So we went up to a place called Polance [phoen], and there had been -- there was a house where an old woman was mistreated and we went to talk to her. And I didn't understand much because everything was in Albanian and at that time I really didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, but the question that was put to the witness is being answered in a rather round about way, and I would suggest that the witness confine herself to the question put, which was: "What did you observe?" Thus far, we have not had any discussion about any observation. I understand, of course, that there is latitude with regard to answering questions; however, it is really not responsive to the question asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the way in which the witness introduced her answer was fully appropriate; and of course the witness, as she did until now, will carefully listen to the question and respond to it as directly as possible. But to say where you went and why you went somewhere before you give the observations you made at that place is fully appropriate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could perhaps make it a little bit more direct --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and just tell us where you went and why you went there.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Okay. In more general terms, not when I actually went the first time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Answer the question as you deem fit. If there's any problem, you'll hear from us. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Right. Okay. So the first time doesn't seem to be very relevant for this case. But when I went there, there were already -- there were -- people were fairly agitated. It was -- the atmosphere was rather tense, and the people I talked to - I can't even remember exactly who I talked to first - but everyone was talking about general insecurity and about increased traffic on the roads at night and seeing people that they had not seen before. And they were not -- they didn't live in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the Chamber anticipates my objection. The answer given is one of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hearsay is not, in general terms, disallowed here. So if a witness gives hearsay evidence, Mr. Guy-Smith, there's -- first of all, the Chamber would be aware of that, and of course we'll take that into consideration. Mr. Re, of course, is instructed if the factual basis is unclear or insufficiently clear to further explore that matter - and of course the Defence also has an opportunity at a later stage to further examine the witness on the factual basis of the testimony - the Chamber would highly appreciate, Mr. Guy-Smith, to start with, to let the flow of information go as uninterrupted as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. The reason that I did choose to rise was because of the specific language used: "I can't remember exactly who I talked to first, but everyone was talking ..." And keeping in mind the instructions that you had given earlier today, it is for that reason, and that reason alone, that I stood. I fully appreciate that hearsay is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Guy-Smith, the instruction of course primarily is for the examining counsel. So before the witness had finished her answer, you had objected already, where Mr. Re did not even have an opportunity to further inquire into who, how many, people told to the witness what she said that was told to her by -- I don't know whether she said "everybody" or "most of the people." But let's try to keep the flow of evidence as uninterrupted as possible. Mr. Re has certainly understood my instructions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just in general terms, what was the general insecurity people told you about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. There was a woman in Klina that told me about having been stopped in January. Late at night, she was travelling with her husband, and there was another car with her brother and her brother's family. And they were stopped late at night by men in uniforms who wanted to check their IDs. A similar incident was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there. Did she tell you the ethnicity or the identity of the men in uniforms who stopped her?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She said that they talked in Albanian; but then when they realised that they were not Albanians, then they talked to them in Serbian. They asked them for their IDs. They asked if there were any police or any weapons in the cars and then they released them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the woman tell you whether these men identified themselves as belonging to any organisation, or whether she was able to say whether they belonged to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She said they were in uniforms, but they were not police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there anything else of any significance that people told you on your first trip to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. There was another -- I mean, all the first interviews -- and at that time what most people seemed to have experienced, is they were either stopped, late night, on the road. There was another incident close to -- closer to Pec. But it was -- it seemed to be always on the more remote roads and late at night. And then the next thing was is the beginning of March is where some people experienced attacks in their houses. There were no casualties. But this would be either a hand grenade thrown into their yard, as was the case, I think, in the village of Pec --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to try to take you through chronologically, if I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have we finished with your first trip to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. That's not relevant for here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was your second trip to Kosovo? Can you give us the date?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: My second trip was end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who did you go to Kosovo with?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: End of March, I travelled to Pristina alone; but then the villages I visited, I visited with another friend, a colleague, who was working at the HLC.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: A colleague from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to give the Court his name or her name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I could but I'd rather -- I cannot implicate other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I won't --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I could give you the name. I don't know what the rules are. You have to advise me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The rules are quite simple, that you answer the questions. If you have any concern about giving names, where you feel that by giving names in public that you might engage any risk for those people, you could ask us whether you could give those names in private session. We'll then consider that request and either allow you or not allow you to give the names in private session, which means that the public will not hear the name you are giving. Of course, the parties will hear it, but it's not relayed to the outside world. And everyone in this courtroom is under an obligation to keep it where it is. So if that sufficiently clarifies -- so if you would say -- I mean, whether you implicate someone, that's another matter. We'd like to hear the answers to the questions as precisely as possible. But I leave it to Mr. Re to what extent the name here is -- whether he wants to press -- to get an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't press you for the name. Was it a colleague from the HLC?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell us where you went and how you got there. Just confine yourself to that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. We went to -- to the village of Ratis, where I went to see a couple --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where you went and how you got there. How did you get from Pristina to Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: From Pristina to Ratis, I travelled in the car with my colleague. She was driving the car. This is an HLC car, or was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter with you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any police presence -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. Which road did you take to travel from Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, we kept to the main roads. We went via Pec/Peje and Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any police presence or roadblocks or road checks between Pristina and Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was at Komarane, there's always been a checkpoint. But I think we just passed through there, but we were stopped in Decane, right in front of the police station. We were stopped, and the car was searched, and we were asked for IDs. But then they let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see any presence of any armed Albanians at any point between Pristina and Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Did you have your notebook with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you recorded the date of when you went to Ratis on your second trip to Kosovo in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't recall recording the date, but I do know the date was probably 28th or 29th of March, or thereabouts, because there had been another incident, and we were supposed to go to Glodjane but then I didn't. I changed my mind and went to Ratis instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I went to Ratis to talk to Culafic couple, to the old couple that lived there and whose house had been under attack one evening a few weeks earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is how did you get the information that led you to go to Ratis, of all places in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. Well, this is -- this is where -- where we follow the press first, and that was one of the names that had been mentioned, one of the families allegedly attacked then. And so that was -- that was the first start.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the effect of the press report that you-- that led you to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: There was a report in different press, and as I recall there -- there were several names of several villages and several families whose houses had allegedly been attacked in between 28th of February and, I think, 5th of March or something. That was the first -- that was the first round, the first time, that we started to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of those whose houses were supposed to have been attacked?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, these people were mostly ethnic Serbs living in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it -- did you have any information about who was supposed to have attacked them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The -- the information in the press was that that was by -- by about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry for interrupting, and I'm very conscious of the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- that you've indicated that interruptions should be kept to a minimum, and I will endeavour to do that. But since this is the first occasion on which Mr. Re has sought to elicit multiple hearsay, that is to say, what was said by someone through a journalist published in a newspaper read by this witness, I'm simply inviting Your Honours' guidance as to whether that is material which you would wish to have elicited or whether it transgresses the guidelines that you have laid down. Obviously, once it's clear how Your Honours wish to proceed, then I shan't raise the issue on multiple occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not disallow these kinds of answers. At the same time, the Defence should be fully aware that if a witness tells us that the reason for her to go somewhere would be publications in the press, and even if she says that the press said that it was the KLA or anyone else, that, of course, the Chamber would not rely on -- I mean, if that's in evidence, that would not lead this Chamber to conclude that, therefore, it was the KLA. We understand this testimony in this context, and that's perhaps a bit different from what you would expect from a jury, but not, since the words are there, that therefore this is conclusive evidence as to who was supposed to do what. It's newspaper material which led the witness to go somewhere, and she explains what she read in the newspaper. That's the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for the clarification. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I think it was fully appropriate here to seek guidance. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there anything said about who had attacked them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: What the Court may like to understand is that these were people in their late 60s --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. The question I'm asking you about was the newspaper report. The question has gone long from the screen, and I can't remember what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, of course, if there's any direct evidence on the attack, of course, would it not be preferable to hear that, rather than to see what -- whether the newspaper reported on it correctly; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was only for completeness, but I'm getting straight to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, I want take you to something you said earlier and then I'll come back to that. You said a little earlier that you were supposed to go to Glodjane but you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. There had been an incident where a police officer was killed and then some ethnic Albanians were killed, and there was some fighting. And then there was supposed to be a funeral. This was 20-something -- I mean, it was so long ago. The 24th or the 28th, somewhere in that period. And I was supposed to go with two of my colleagues from Pristina, but for some reason I thought I rather should not. And I cannot explain this. There was nothing that had led me to believe that I shouldn't go except an internal feeling that I should not go. And so I didn't. I went to Ratis and interviewed Culafics instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I want you to tell the Court who you interviewed, the Culafics, and where interviewed them and what they told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, perhaps first, you said there had been an incident where a police officer was killed and some ethnic Albanians were killed. Was this information that you received from the press as well or from -- from what source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The -- the incident was general knowledge because it was in the news. But there was also another of my colleagues who was working at HLC. She was in close contact with the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, that was another organisation based in Pristina, that was following different human rights violations and incidents involving the state and ethnic Albanians throughout the troubles in the 1990s. So she knew when the funeral was going to be. And I think she'd also, I'm not sure, but I think she'd also talked to somebody in Glodjane before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, the incident was general knowledge. That would include the ethnicity -- you said it was on the news, I take it, by the media. Then you say some ethnic Albanians were killed. Was that part of media reporting as well, that these were the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was -- I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's fine. No, no --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I think that four or five ethnic Albanians were killed and a police officer was shot dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you said there was some fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was fighting because then more police went into the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the source of the information for the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of it was in the news and some of it came from -- from my colleagues who were working in Pristina in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you explained already how you became aware of the funeral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re. This is -- by the way, this is the kind of exercise I had in mind if the factual basis of knowledge is not perfectly clear. You're the first witness in this case, so we -- it's not only new for you, but we have to find our ways of getting your evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you -- where did you speak to the couple in Ratis?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I spoke at their house, in Ratis, and they showed me where the -- what is that -- something is propelled. I'm not sure what, the thing that goes from one shoulder. It left a hole this big --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. I'll just stop you there. You're holding your hands up about 15 centimetres apart, in a circle.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. It's like circle like that, up -- right underneath the roof. And it went through their house. No one was hurt. This was in the evening, so they could not see the attackers. And the man said that there was also -- Mr. Culafic also said that there was automatic fire, and I could see some bullets on the side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you had your notebook. Did you record what they told you in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have your notebook here with you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. What were the names of the people -- these two people you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Jela Culafic and Nastadin. They also called him Malisa. But he was a big man; he wasn't small.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. I want you to have a look on the screen at Exhibit 693, pages 16 to 19 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you give a number to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see it in front of you? Can you see something on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, we first would need a number for -- an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First of all, the thing on the screen, just for the record, can you identify that as a copy of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, Madam Registrar, I think that we would give numbers immediately, MFI numbers, so that ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit number P1, I marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, just what I'm doing is I'll be showing the witness the diaries which are 65 ter Exhibit 693, 694, 695 and 696 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you want to tender them into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, and taking her to extracts in them. That was my intention, to identify extracts in the diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, if you -- you say you want to tender these documents as exhibits. So, therefore, in order to avoid whatever confusion, they should receive a number right away. And we now have P1 in front of us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can take you to what's on the screen in front of you. There's a -- I actually want to take you to page 16 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's always teething problems the first time we do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what I want you to do is to look at that and to tell us whether that's a translation of the notes you took in your conversation with Mr. and Mrs. Culafic on --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Culafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- in late March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it pretty much is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The relevant pages go that one, the next one, and the one afterwards. As Your Honour will see with e-court, you've got to go from page to page to find them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've got page 16 on the screen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you -- who were the next people you spoke to after speaking to the -- that couple?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Next I spoke to the son of the police officer that had been killed in Ratis a few weeks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The family name was Prascevic, but I'm not sure I can remember the son's name. There's a very short note, I think before this page. The killed -- the man that was killed was called Slobodan Prascevic. I spoke to his son but I can't quite recall whether he was Milan or Milovan, something like that. Prascevic was the name. I also spoke with Prascevic's daughter and wife, but they were quite confused and this was still -- they were grieving, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the effect of what they told you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, the effect was that -- I'm sorry, I don't understand. You mean with the assassination of the police or attacks on houses and farms?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The attacks on houses.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Okay, right. So later on, after Culafic family, I spoke with a few families from the villages in that general area were close to. I spoke to the man in Lug Bunar, in Bec, in Crmljane, and all these attacks happened between the 28th of February and the 5th of March. And in Crmljane, one of the families that lived -- Babovic, they lived at the very end of the village, very remote place, the man claimed that their house had been shot at twice; once on the 28th of February, and the second time was the 5th of March -- or was it the 1st of March, 5th of March, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They were all ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they tell you who had shot at them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They didn't know exactly because most of these attacks would happen at night. But generally, everyone claimed that they had already been an armed guerrilla group and they attributed attacks to them. At that time, very early, nobody had seen people or seen their attackers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I -- in e-court, can we just go back to the fifth page of the exhibit currently displayed, and in the middle of the page, in the English, there's a heading called Prascevic interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The first line says, "The police are not allowed to enter Jablanica. The son suspects the terrorists had done this and he sent a man." Can you tell the Chamber what that's about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This is something very, very complicated. I don't understand how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just a moment. Just a line was read to you by Mr. Re saying: "The police are not allowed to enter Jablanica." Is that what someone said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what the son said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says Prascevic interview. Is what's recorded there the contents of your interview with the son of Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, the interview had been interrupted by a telephone call, and I don't know what he thought, but then all of a sudden he stopped talking and, I guess you could say, sent me packing. Because it was one of my colleagues from Pristina had called, and I think he was nervous because my colleague was Albanian and she spoke with an accent. So unfortunately ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm interested in the source of the information, "the police are not allowed to enter Jablanica." Was that something he told you or something --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. His father was a police officer. And if I recall -- I don't quite remember, but if I recall right, I think he was also with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you go down a little, it says: "Dragoslav Stojanovic was stopped on the road. He works in the school in Dubrava. A group from Albanian had taken his brother Vlado across the border, beat him up and took his saw and weapons." Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This is also what Mr. Prascevic told me. But later on I spoke to these people. These were two separate incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next information in the diary says: "Three hundred houses, a pure Serbian village; the remaining 18 villages are Albanian. On 28 February 1998, an incident occurred." Above that it says, "Mr. Zvonko Kolasinac."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. That was the man that I talked to, the man that was beaten up on the road between Gorazde and Pec. That was another person that I interviewed at about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could go four pages over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you also, what is said here, "three hundred houses," et cetera, that's all what he told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's -- the one I want you to go to has an 8 at the bottom of the page, and the date -- says Monday, the 2nd of March, 1998. All right. Without -- without looking at the name on the top, is it possible to -- okay. There's information there, and there's someone's name on the top. Is that -- it says: "Monday, 2 March 1998, Sloba told me to take my son and the vehicle and come to Rznic." Now, there's a lot of information there. I'm not going to take you to all of them -- all of it. But what was the effect, the summary, of what you were told here and what you recorded.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. Well, this woman claimed that she had been in the car when this police officer was killed, and it was also her son was in the car. I spoke with her when she was still at the hospital in Pec, because she had been wounded. She had also told -- she also told me that later on that same day, that there was a group of armed men around her house, and that her children who had been -- the rest of her children who had been in the house had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did she say who the armed men were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She didn't. She said they were armed but she never identified them as one group or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given any information which could have allowed you to conclude who they were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Armed men, you know, in that general area, I would have thought that that was the -- the guerrillas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we go to the page, which is page 23 of that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because there's a pause, I don't believe I am breaking the flow, I'd interpose an objection. Lack of foundation. Also, the answer is speculative and is not something which should be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you could perhaps move down and go to Radenko Fatic, Crmljane, 3rd of April, 1998. I'll just leave it there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's some entries in your diary which suggest you were in Kosovo on the 3rd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I went to Crmljane and that's where I spoke with Radenko Fatic. I spoke with him at his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to Crmljane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Because that was one of the villages that was listed as alleged -- one of the alleged attacks on Serbian families in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the information you had that led you to go to that particular village? Where did you obtain the information and what was the information?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This was all -- I think this was all in the press. There was a list of villages that were named, and then I tried to get to some of them and talk to at least some of the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell us about the interview with Radenko Fatic on the 3rd of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fatic said that the attack came at night and that he claimed to -- to have recognised his next-door neighbour. He would not tell me the name. In fact, I recall that he said, "I will tell to people who need to know." But -- but he also said that the two other houses were under attack that same night. And then I went to see the other -- the other person, Mr. Babovic. And then there was a third house where there were two old people, but I -- I didn't find them, they were not at home. If I recall well, they had children elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your notes also record that you met a Pera Delic, D-e-l-i-c, on the 3rd of April, 1998. Where did you meet Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I met him at his home in Lug Bunar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: He told me a very similar story, that that was -- that somebody had shot at their house. It was night and he had -- I think he had his hunting rifle or something. But he didn't see exactly -- exactly see the attackers because it was dark, so he could not see clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can e-court just go back one page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Looking at page 22 of Exhibit 693 --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- does that record your interview with Mr. Pera Delic or someone else in the family?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That was Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next one I want to go to is -- if I can approach it this way. You were there in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many people did you interview or how many places did you go to in April -- about that time, April 3rd, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The first -- you know, it was in the villages of -- I went to Ratis. I spoke to people in Decane. I met with several of the Stojanovic family. I talked to these two families in Crmljane. I talked to Mr. Delic in Lug Bunar. I spoke with an elderly man. There were three houses in Bec, and all houses were allegedly attacked with hand-grenade attacks. Again, no casualties. But I spoke with two people. And I'm not sure. I believe they were -- there were Djukic, Mitic, and I think Lakic. There's a mistake in the translation. Probably they couldn't read it -- read my handwriting. These were the three families. And there was -- I think it was the old man -- I think that was Mr. Mitic. And then a younger man came to -- came to collect his father and take him to Djakovica, because they felt it was not safe to stay there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell us about when you spoke to Mr. Djakovic. Was that in Bec?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can we just go to page 23, which is the next page of the diary, at the very top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this, in fact, the interview with Mr. Djakovic from Bec?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says -- the heading is Djakovica. "We now live in Djakovica and we can no longer leave. This was between 28 and 1 March, around 1.15 hours, three bombs were thrown in that direction." And so on.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information there, just to clarify it, was what Mr. Djakovic told you.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Was there any -- were you given any other information when you were there which enabled you to draw any conclusions as to who was the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No. That was not, because that was -- that was at night and it was in the dark, and this place is really -- you know, it's almost in the woods, these three houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The answer is no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that an appropriate time, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's approximately one hour and a half after we started this afternoon. Before we adjourn, however, Mr. Re, in terms of timing, of course we spent some time in the beginning on procedural issues, but the witness has been scheduled for two hours, I think, in chief, which would mean that you would finish during the next session. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. As I read it, I've had one hour and I've got one more to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. In the next session. We would then, after one hour, because that brings me to my next question. The Defence earlier indicated that they reserve the right not to start cross-examination. Is that still your position, or would you consider it a possibility, to at least start cross-examining the witness today? I'm not pushing. I'm just seeking information.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And with the greatest of reluctance and regret, I have to maintain the position that I took yesterday, because the notes that have been provided to us, which this witness is currently using as the basis of her evidence in-chief, is the central thrust of the material that was disclosed to us so late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not pushing. I was just wondering whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At a convenient moment, probably after this witness has finished her examination-in-chief, may we take stock of the witnesses that are coming, when they're coming and the provision of material so that this situation doesn't continue to arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your point. We'll have a break. We'll adjourn and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late return. It was caused by an urgent matter we had to deal with during the break. Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can report back to the Chamber that the protective measures motion has been filed, and I have copies here of another filing which was an annex to another confidential filing. It's a declaration of the investigator. I've given copies to the Defence. Is it appropriate for me to hand it to the Trial Chamber? It is only a copy of the declaration part, not the actual motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, before the break we were talking about your visit to Kosovo in around April the 3rd of 1998. How long were you in Kosovo on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From what you saw and observed, did you -- were you able to draw any conclusions of any activities?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, at that point, the only conclusion that could be drawn was that something was happening in villages, usually in more remote villages and where there were few houses, and -- and little else. I mean, there was -- there was nothing definite that could be concluded at that point. That was still fairly early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, of course, you're not asking for conclusions. You said: "How long were you in Kosovo at that time?" "From what you saw and observed, were you able to draw any conclusions of any activities?" That is a question which is so unspecific that -- and further it asks for conclusions, opinion, rather than facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you report back to the HLC as a result of your visit to Kosovo on the 3rd of April? What was the effect of what you reported back, based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: What I reported back was exactly what people told me, you see, because in the -- in the incident part, we weren't describing things. We could make a note at the end of the text, but we would usually write what people have told us. That was the general principle. And I went a step further and I usually recorded everything verbatim, which means people spoke -- you know, my notes were usually -- people spoke in the dialect, and that's how the reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is, Natasa Kandic had sent you down to Kosovo to look into what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you went back, what did you tell her that you had generally observed about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I told her that the people that I talked to reported that there was increased security [sic], increased activity at night, usually cars going on local roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You said "reported that there was increased security." Maybe the word was recorded incompletely or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Increased? Increased security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Insecurity. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Insecurity, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I reported back what -- what the notes -- exactly what the notes say; that is, the people that I talked to have alleged that they have been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your notes indicate that you spoke to people on the 9th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that in Kosovo or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That was -- that was in Kosovo. Now, I really can't recall whether that was the same trip or I went back to Belgrade and then returned to Kosovo after -- a few days later. I really can't recall that. But on the 9th, yes, I was in Kosovo, and I talked to -- to a number of people then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I went to Djakovica, but I don't think -- I don't recall having made any interviews there. And then I went back to -- to Decane, where I interviewed two people, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. How did you get to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: On a bus. Public transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you observe about the security situation on your trip there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, there was very little to observe, unusual. I mean, at that time there were checkpoints in usual places, usual for whoever travelled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you elaborate --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on what you mean by "the usual places"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, the usual places, like, there would be a big checkpoint going from Pristina to Pec/Peje. There was a big checkpoint at Komarane; then there was another one at Decane. And then around Djakovica, that depended. But the public transport was still operating, so I travelled on public buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your notes indicate that you interviewed some people called Stojanovic on the 9th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I interviewed them in Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you interview them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Because I had heard that the -- that after the incident in Glodjane earlier, at the end of March, that they have moved from their village, from their house in Dubrava, to -- to Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the 33rd page of the present exhibit please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is always the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of the translation. Can we go down the page, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says "9th of April, Vlad," and Stojanovic is crossed out, and it says "Filip". I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber about what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Right. This is not an interview with Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page -- or two pages along, I'm sorry, page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this the correct interview?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The next one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Have a look at that. Is -- does that record your interview with Mr. Stojanovic? It says "Dubrava: It was Tuesday" --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- "24th of March this year."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "My mother and my brother were there. I took my four-year-old son." When it says "there," where are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They're referring to -- to their village, to their home in the village of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it says: "I suddenly heard firing."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they tell you who was doing the firing?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please just go down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It says on the page before the Court, which is marked at page 10 on the exhibit: "They opened fire on the next-door neighbours where about 20 soldiers were based. When I passed through the village, I noticed that in Glodjane, no one from the neighbours wanted to say hello that day." What sort of soldiers was Mr. Stojanovic referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I have to read it, if you would just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just for your guidance, in order to avoid whatever confusion, the question would have been phrased better if you would have asked the witness what the -- whether the interlocutor of the witness explained what soldiers he was referring to, because if you're asking what soldiers was he referring to, then it leaves open that the witness makes conclusions without us even noticing. So, therefore, would you please phrase the questions very precisely in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be easier to show the witness the original of her notes for her to remember this answer, her notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, you said earlier you have a copy of your notes with you in the court.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it assists, how quickly can you find the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I'll try to be fairly quick. Yes. In the original, Mr. Stojanovic just says that in the house next to him, that there were 20 soldiers. He did not refer what sort of soldiers. He said that there was -- they were shooting at the police and the other way around. There was shooting between 20 soldiers and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given information from anyone else as to who these soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It was the general understanding, and at the time all the people were talking about the Kosovo Liberation Army, but this I -- I don't know. I mean, he just said "20 soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you also speak to his mother?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we go to the 39th page of this particular exhibit, please. I'm sorry, 36 -- page 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you please instruct the witness; otherwise I'll do that. Witness, you said it was a general understanding, and all -- at the time all the people were talking about the Kosovo Liberation Army, but you say you don't know. The mere fact that you don't know is sufficient. If Mr. Re would like to elicit from you what you heard people talking about, he'll specifically ask you to whom did you speak, what did they tell you, what questions did they put. But if there's an answer where you say I don't know, I mean, what the rumours were and what the general knowledge was is not something we could draw any conclusions from at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
