utterances.text: Go to the bottom of the page on page 36. Who is that referring to? It says "LJS: Have been on the land for 75 years, 65 years. They did not attack me. I intended to return there. Until the police came, I was with them everyday."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Those are -- what is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is that referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That is -- that refers to Mrs. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, she said that she was at home and that they were -- since they were the only house in ten villages, that occasionally -- actually, quite frankly, twice a week approximately there would be a police patrol that would come and visit just to check on her and see if she was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say the only house in ten villages, what are you talking about, the "only house"? Are you talking about ethnicity or something else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah. She claimed that that was the only ethnic Serb house in ten villages around. I don't know if that was quite correct, but that is what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did she tell you whether anything had happened to her or her family?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She said that at -- she didn't specify the date, but she said that her son, who was visiting with her, told everyone to get into the house, and then she heard shooting outside, and she saw some police, and then she said that they were under -- that there was fire exchanged for -- for a while, until the evening, and then they were taken to -- to Decane, out of -- out of their -- their house in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is "they," and who took them to Decane, and when?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It was her two sons, herself, and -- and the grandson, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know the grandson's name, but her sons were -- one was Vladimir; the other one was Mijat. It may be that Dragoslava was there as well. I don't recall. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did she tell you, or did anyone tell you, who the fire exchange was between?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She didn't see that. She didn't see who exactly was -- was shooting, but she knew that they had been -- that earlier that day, that the police were shot at. And then it seems that the family - that's what they said - the family radioed the police, who then sent another patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who took them to Decane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I presume it was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did she tell you why they went there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if the witness says, "I presume it was," you should ask the witness, then, if she presumes that, what is the basis of this presumption? You may understand that we're trying to elicit from you, first of all, what you observed yourself. Of course, part of your work was to conduct interviews, so we'll hear about the interviews as well. But if a question is put to you, who brought them there and you say, "I presume it was the police," it could be because you were told it was the police, or it was because you concluded from the whole of the situation, and all these matters should be entirely clear to us from which -- from what basis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you tell us that it was presumably the police. And if it's just conclusions and presumptions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we might even limit ourselves to what is of greater interest to us, and that's your personal observation and the direct results of your interviews. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber wants me to clarify with you the basis of your presumption. You said you presumed it was the police. As briefly as you possibly can, why do you say you presume it was the police?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The basis for the presumption was -- I'm not sure, but I think that's what her son told me. They were all together. Because I can't find it here. I don't see it in the notes on the interview with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What information, if any, were you given about her sons Dragoslav and Mijat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: At that time she mentioned that her son Dragoslav had been stopped a few weeks earlier on the road and that he was -- he was asked whether he had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stopped by whom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Stopped by armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Were you given any information as to who the armed men were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: She said that they asked him where he was from and searched his car and found a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is about whether she gave you any information as to who the armed men were.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: What she claimed was that there were armed men and that they were carrying -- that they were masked, as she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given any information about anything happening to Dragoslav and Mijat later?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That was later on. I talked also to Dragoslav, but much, much later. I talked to a cousin of theirs who went back to the village a few days later to collect some -- some things, and that was, I think, round the -- mid-April, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it mid-April you had the conversation or mid-April you were told it occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It was mid-April -- mid-April that that had occurred. I think I talked to them after Easter, immediately after Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you talked to a cousin of theirs. Who was the cousin?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Could I have a look at his name? Because I'm getting to be a bit tired. I can't remember whether the name was Stijovic or something, but they went back to the village together, according to him, and they were detained for a few hours and beaten up and then taken back to the road. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given any information about who detained them and who beat them up?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That was -- they said that there were armed people in Glodjane and they were taken to Glodjane, and that was the first time that I heard the name, what I thought was Haradini or Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this in your diary?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It is somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In what context were you told the name Haradini or Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: As I recall, it was in the context that that was the person that they recognised or that they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you told had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I was told that they were taken from their house to a house in Glodjane, and that then they were questioned and beaten up, especially Dragoslav Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where does the Haradini or Haradinaj name come from in the context of what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That was the name that they mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In what context did they mention the name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In the context that -- that was the man that they -- that they -- that was coming in and out of that room and that seemed to have some sort of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what room was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I please interrupt here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you just told us, is that what the cousin told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because you referred to "they" just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that was the name "they" mentioned. Now, I tried to understand your testimony as good as I can; that is, the cousin, if I did understand you well, describes how not he alone, but together with the persons you mentioned and was taken to a house, and then you said "that was the name they mentioned." And it is perfectly unclear to me whether this was the name the cousin told you or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Could you be very precise in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to be, but it's been eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't remember, then please tell us. Everyone will understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm confusing the Court, there's-- because that was when -- when this incident -- after this incident happened, I talked to several people, not at the same time, but in that particular situation, there was a lot of agitation, because there were -- a lot of families were leaving their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I perhaps stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you talked to many people. Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you talked about a cousin. Who were the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm trying to find these particular pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could assist the Trial Chamber and refer to 65 ter number 694 and the 20th page of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can see on the screen in front of you, does that assist? It says: "Stojanovic Mijat, Dragoslav. It was before Easter when we set off in two weeks. Veselin Stijovic, a cousin, was with us when we noticed two or three men." Who was it you were speaking to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I was speaking to Mijat because Dragoslav -- I was told that Dragoslav was at the hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information you've recorded there about someone called Nasim Haradinaj and a beating and throwing them into a courtyard, taking their documents, and so on --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- was that information given to you by the cousin?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I think this was the interview with Mijat. I also talked to Stijovic, but at this point I can't recall whether it was then or later on in September when I went back. And I also talked to Dragoslav Stojanovic, after he'd come out of hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you meet the two, do you recall? Oh, I'm sorry. I said -- Dragoslav Stojanovic. When did you meet Dragoslav Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I met Dragoslav later -- later in the year. It could have been September, late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you record your notes or interview in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I haven't seen it in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your notes say that on the 22nd of April, they refer to you being in Belgrade and meeting a Roma man called Ramadan Uka, or Nezaj.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your circumstances of meeting this Roma man in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if you take the witness to a certain portion of her notes, the Chamber would be happy to know exactly where to find it so that we can follow you. And, by the way, when you refer to the other document on which we are now on page 20, it needed a number because it was not the original document we had in front of us earlier. Madam Registrar, that would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit Number P2, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Re, could you take us to the page, and could you also be very precise also in your questioning. I mean, you could assist the witness in being as detailed as possible, and I'll stand corrected as well where I earlier said that the witness said that she talked to many people; you said to several people only, so I made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The exhibit we're on at the moment, P2, MFI --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And also at the top of page 2 which may assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It records: "22nd of April, Djakovica, Uk Nexhaj from Budisavci, near Pec."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just go to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you interview this person?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I talked to Ramadan because the -- a Roma organisation from Belgrade, their local organisation -- I don't even know what they're called. They are a Roma association of some sort or other. They came and said they were Roma refugees from Kosovo in a particular place, in a settlement, provision -- you know, cardboard-box settlement, near the Sava River in Belgrade, so I went down to see them, to see what -- their circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've recorded information there about the aunt coming out and asking who it was in Albanian, them breaking the door; one of them was carrying an automatic. Were you given any information as to who these people were, the ones who came to the door with the automatic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Ramadan said -- claimed that he knew some of them, and later on that page you can find names, as I wrote them down. This is what I heard from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are three names written on the next page which is on the screen. It says: "Vilson, Kitaj, and Buq Veselaj." Are they the names you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Underneath it says: "The other Roma are scared of the Albanians." What was the information you have about which Albanians they're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That's what the man said. He didn't specify and he didn't -- he didn't specify who exactly. He -- for the most part, he talked about what happened to his family and how they left under threat and didn't feel secure to remain in Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he tell you why the Roma feared the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: He gave, you know, this other reason, that they were -- some people felt threatened -- felt that they had to go to the polls in the previous election that was not recognised by the state. But his predominant fear was what happened to them and the threat that they received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When he spoke about Albanians, was he talking about Albanians in general or specific Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I would not like to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Were you in April -- were you in Belgrade in mid-April 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any media reports causing your organisation any interest?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were a series of reports in April about different families being attacked in villages, usually in villages where there were only a few houses. But for this particular case, as far as Ramadan is concerned, this was something that we were referred to by this Roma organisation, because they knew about them and brought some aid to the family as the first -- you know, as a first aid kit, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. You said about different families being attacked in villages. What do you mean by "different families"?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Different families were -- there were families in several villages, and I later on, on the -- after Easter, I interviewed some of them. There were incidents involving family, as I recall, family Jukic. I talked to the sister of these two men; they were brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to -- what I'm after at the moment is there were different families. Was it something to do with their ethnicity or something else?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They were -- usually they were ethnic Serbs, at the moment -- at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As a result of your organisation hearing about these media reports, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I was sent out to Decane to try and speak with some of these families.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: To Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This was on the 20-something April. I think that Easter was on the 19th, and then that would have been -- Easter Monday. That would have been Tuesday or Wednesday after Easter --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: -- of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I went on a bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: -- from Pristina, and then from Pristina to Pec, and then from Pec to Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you observe of the security situation on the road to Decane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The first thing that I saw that there was a lot of police at the police station, and then I walked to where the -- where I'd previously talked to a few people. This -- there was these small wooden huts that used to be this sort of youth camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: -- and I'd heard from people in Decane that there would be villagers who had fled their villages, that they would be there. And so I went up the road where I knew that they would be, and again I saw a lot of police and I was turned back. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who turned you back?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts did they turn you back?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: As I was going up, up the hill where this youth -- former youth camp used to be. So I went back to Decane, but by the time I got back there, which is about half a kilometre each way, I think word already spread that there was somebody who would interview people, who wanted to talk to them, and so I talked to a number of them in Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm -- I'm just interested in the police turning you back at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you going, and why did they turn you back?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I was going to this youth camp, and the police turned me back because they didn't want me to be there, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they give you a reason?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: No, they actually didn't. They just told me to go right back where I came from and wouldn't let me go to the -- up to the camp, all the way to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that particular trip to Kosovo, did you observe any military presence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Military? No. At that point, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just for my clarification, when you're talking about the police, you're talking about the regular police forces who at that moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, regular police force, state police, Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many people did you interview in this former youth camp?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't interview them at the camp because I went back to Decane. But then I must have talked to about half a dozen that I really talked to individually, because at first --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. One step at a time.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you interview them?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: There was a little cafe just off the main --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A cafe in Decane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: In Decane, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Next step. How many people did you interview? Just the figures.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know, five, six.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They were from villages in the Decane area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which villages?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Some were from Pozar, some from Ljubarda. There were some from -- I think even from Papracane. Mainly villages from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: All of them were ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you record what they told you in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the effect of what they were telling you about what had happened to them and why they were in Decane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: The general feeling was everybody was very agitated. Some of them had been stopped before, like a few days before. Some had been taken by armed men and questioned and then released. And there was a general feeling of insecurity, and most of them felt that they could not stay in their villages, mainly due to the fact that they were fairly -- there were fairly few houses. And there was a general feeling of insecurity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fairly few houses of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Of Kosovar Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one -- may I, Mr. Re. You say that there was a general feeling of insecurity, "and most of them felt that they could not stay in their villages." Now, you told us that you spoke to five or six people. When you say "most of them," is it that you're talking about four out of these five or four out of these six, or is it that you're telling us that they said that others, perhaps in similar circumstances or different circumstances, that -- were they reporting on what they observed to be kind of a general feeling or are you telling us that most of them, that is, most of the people you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the people I interviewed claimed that there was a sense of insecurity, increasing insecurity, and that they could not stay safely in their villages and that they wanted to leave and -- especially if they had children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they speaking just for themselves or were they, in a way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were speaking for themselves but also for others. These are small communities. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us how they exactly expressed that. I can imagine that, speaking for themselves, they would have said something like, I feel that it's not safe here; I can't stay in my village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did they refer to what they claimed was a feeling among others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they would -- they would mention -- one of the people - now I wish I could find his name - but he said that he was stopped and then -- and that the -- that he saw armed men on the tractor two days previously. I think he was the -- I think his name was Cepanovic from Pozar, but my memory may not be precise. Then, for example, the sister of these two Jukic brothers, she said that somebody shot at their house a few nights before, and because they had children, they didn't feel it was safe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but they were still then speaking for themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is what they said exactly as far as the general feeling of insecurity of others was concerned. What did they tell you? Because you're saying they were not talking just about themselves but they were also talking about others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They would say that -- because people were stopped and because they've been -- there have been shooting incidents at their houses, they felt that they could not stay. And they were afraid, especially, you know, after dark. And there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke to an elderly man who was stopped with -- he was travelling with, I think, another relative, female relative, and they were stopped and they were taken to Glodjane, if I recall right. And he claimed -- he was not mistreated or anything, but he and his female cousin were kept there for a couple of hours and then they were released. And that was -- that was what made him decide that it was safer, at least for a while -- I understood that people thought that that would be for a while, that they would be -- for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is still about what people told you why they felt unsafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the sixth page of the current exhibit please be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- I think your diary records you speaking to someone called Uros Labovic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Uros Labovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you -- was he one of the people that you spoke to in that cafe in Decane?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did he tell you -- sorry, first of all, where was he from?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't recall. He was from one of those villages, but I can't recall now whether it was Papracane or Pozar or it was -- or Ljubarda. It was one of the villages from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Could I refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: -- to my notes. I'm sorry, I'm getting a bit tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you refer to us to the right page in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is that the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That would be a help for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That might be a little difficult at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I just mean to make it a little easier for the witness. I mean the witness then could see it on the screen in her original handwriting. That would help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may, but she has a copy of them in her hands there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: A copy of which she has to find the right page, doesn't she. This is my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I agree entirely. Ideally I would have the two of them sorted together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If you would have the ERN number, that would be fine, too. Then we could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may assist. I think it's -- I think it's -- it bears the ERN number is stamped in red, of U0030259.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, would that number help you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it would, because I seem to have an original that is not full and that doesn't have all the things that are in the translation. So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I mean we could show that on the screen, ERN number U0030259. I have it on the screen now, but -- yes, that's it. That would be the one. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although -- right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe the next page would help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, if you would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, right. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that help your recollection --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- of speaking to Uros Labovic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Labovic was talking about the insecurity, and then also word spread that nobody knows what happened to a number of elderly people who have left -- who were left behind in villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Elderly people of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Elderly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could have the English translation back on the screen for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the top it says: "Did people ever return to Babaloc, Milovic, Djurkovic," et cetera. Is that the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says: "19th of April the KLA controlled the Decane-Djakovica road. On the 20th of April the refugees are returning to Babaloc? 21 April refugees in Babaloc visit from UNHCR. 22 April, visit of the HCR/Pristina is scheduled." What's all that about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That's what we were trying at HLC, we were trying to establish the chronology of events and information that we were receiving from different sources, whether it was in the news or whether through the people that I interviewed or some of my colleagues or, indeed, information from other organisations, such as the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The entry: "19th of April, the KLA controls the Decane-Djakovica road," what's the source of your information for that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: That is what -- okay. There were two sources of information. One was in the news and the other one was it seemed that that weekend -- that that was the weekend where most people fled, or immediately after that, fled the villages and went to Decane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What you've written is quite precise. "The KLA controls the Decane-Djakovica road." Why did you write that precise piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This was general knowledge. It was what people were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which people?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: People in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: People of which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "general knowledge," you mean it was what people were telling you, what you were hearing on the radio, or what?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: What we were hearing on the radio and also what some people would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And which people are you referring to when you say --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I'm referring to ethnic Serbs who lived in these -- in that general area, in rural area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the next one, where it says: "The refugees are referring to Babaloc" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, before we continue here, the witness told us that there were two sources; the first was the press and the second one, she said it was about the 19th of April, it's immediately after that that the people started -- what did she exactly say? Let me try to find it. One was the news, and the other was: "it seems that that weekend that was the weekend where most people fled." So there one part is source and the other one is -- has got nothing to do with source. Now, the type of knowledge you need to come to a conclusion that the KLA controls the Decane-Djakovica road, that's a rather complex conclusion. Therefore, if you do not further explore that, then it sounds -- and perhaps I could ask you. I'm not blaming you for anything at all, but this Chamber, of course, has the duty to see exactly what you observed, what others observed. It sounds that -- as if you had -- from what you heard from people, from what you read in the newspapers, that without knowing exactly on what basis people would come to a conclusion that the KLA was controlling a road, which is a -- well, you need to know exactly who is on that road, who is not on that road, how do you control the road; that this was what -- was rumour that spread around that KLA controlled that road. Is it anything more, anything specific that you said? That: "People were telling me that on that road, which is 20 kilometres long, every 2 kilometres they have a" -- whatever. I mean, I'm seeking to find out whether you had any specific knowledge, either by observing yourself or specific knowledge obtained from others, that would explain, whether true or not, but would explain why everyone was thinking that the KLA was in control of that road. Could you give us such specifics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say that I have such specifics. This is what I heard from people in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And without knowing exactly what these people had available as specifics on which they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing that was for certain was that they fled their villages and they were in Decane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's -- you met them there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and they told you that they had fled their villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, having clarified this issue, perhaps you could keep this in the back of your mind when, perhaps, dealing with the other events that are listed here; first of all, to find out whether there's any specific knowledge; if not, then to -- well, then that's at least clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who are the refugees you are referring to? In the next line it says: "The refugees are returning to Babaloc."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: "The refugees from -- returning to Babaloc," that refers to people who were accommodated at the little settlement that was built by UNHCR, and they were mostly people from Albanian, ethnic Serbs and Montenegrins from Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: They sought refuge, I think, when there were disturbances in Albanian, like, a year or two previously. I don't quite remember whether it was in 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could just go down the page, please, scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are some names there that say: "Kidnapped Serbs: Slobodan Radosevic, Milos Radunovic, Milica Radunovic, Milovan Vlahovic, Milka Vlahovic, Dara Vujosevic, Vukosava Vujosevic, Branko Stanatovic."

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: It should say I think Stematovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stematovic --

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you write that there? What was the source of your information? What were you told, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: This was a summary of the names that I got from some of the people that I interviewed and another colleague of mine from -- she also got -- I think she interviewed Vlahovic family or their daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please excuse this unusual interruption on my part, but I'm having a little difficulty following exactly where this comes from in the original notebook, and I don't have the language capacity to follow it. But I am looking at the original notebook at U0030260 and where that overlaps with 0259, and for some reason this whole section appears to be missing and I'm not sure, therefore, whether what we have had photocopied for us in the original notebook form is, in fact, the page sequence of what the witness has in front of her in her original notebook. If not, then there's something very confusing in what we have here in front of us. I don't know if that can be called up on your screens so that you can see the difficulty I'm having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, actually, you're doing, you're trying to find the list of names and you can't find them on these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could help us out, because one would expect a page almost exclusively of dates, names, years of birth -- could you guide us? Where --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll certainly try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, can you look in your notebook there, or the copy of your notebook. Where in it are the names of the kidnapped Serbs noted? In English it appears directly after the evidence you just gave us about meeting Mr. Jovo Slava -- sorry, about the road and the refugees and so on.

utterances.speaker: MARIJANA ANDJELKOVIC.
utterances.text: I shall try and find it for you, although to me it also seems that the copy that I have got is not all that was -- is not all the notebooks. So I really don't know whether they were -- I'll try to find it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, the copy you've got in front of you, is that just a copy of the original or do there also appear some kind of long-type numbers on the pages --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are -- there are long numbers on the pages as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us the -- we just discussed what happened on the 19th of April, 20th of April, return of refugees, et cetera. Could you tell us on what page you exactly find that, and then referring to the stamped number, which is a number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's--

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think it's 003027 -- sorry, U0030273 and 274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, I will try to find that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that, Your Honour, at all, in -- in the copy that I have got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you mind perhaps to give the page -- have you found that, the 19th of April, et cetera, references?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We actually have the originals in court here as well as photocopies, if it may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what we're trying to do is to find out where the -- 0273. Yes. Just for your information, Ms. Andjelkovic, I see that you had in front of you a bundle of photocopies, starting with stamped ERN number, front page without but seems to be a cover page notepad, and then the first written -- handwritten page, 0030163, so just referring to the last three digits, it goes from 163 up to and including 253. I have not checked whether all the pages are there, but it seems, at first sight, rather complete, covering the range I just mentioned. So then the witness has not the original in front of her you were referring to. Now, Mr. Harvey, just to come back to -- you are led to -- guided to pages 273, 274, I think. I'm just trying to find that. I see the -- let me -- I'd like to -- could we have the English version on our screens? Yes. From what I can see at this moment -- could we move up a little bit in the English original? Yes. Now, here, I think, we have the -- identified the problem you are facing, Mr. Harvey, because on the lower part of the original of 273, we find names: The first one with the year of birth 1943; the second one, 60 years. That's -- and that also says that these are -- at least I can recognise more or less the word"Serbs"; I don't know what "kidnapped" is. Now, what we see just above that, we would expect to have one line without dates and then above that a line containing at least 21 and 22; above that, 22 April; above that, a line with 21 April; 20 April. And I cannot find that above the section on kidnapped Serbs, Mr. Re. Therefore, it appears that what is presented as a translation of an original seems to be not a translation of what we find in 273. I'm just referring to the last two -- the last three digits. Can you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for your help in at least locating this passage. I'm also certainly not putting myself forward as a handwriting expert, but I'm just wondering whether, in fact, this is in the handwriting of the witness herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's have now the B/C/S -- let's have the B/C/S version on the screen so the witness can follow. Ms. Andjelkovic, you're totally out of this. We're talking about translations of documents you have provided, and if there's any confusion, you certainly have not, at this point, created any of it. So let's get -- now we have the original. Could you, first of all, perhaps -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: If we would go back to the page ending with 259. I think this was the place we originally had before us, and here we also can discuss the question of who wrote the notes, and maybe this would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: First one thing. Could you give us an information, if all the notes are from your own hand, or is it from different people? Because I see in the last line, "Border incident" in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can now see it and ask it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Page 259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's on your screen. I hope it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And this is also in your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move a bit further down? There we see the dates, and, I take it, the portions of your notes which was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this what you -- are these your -- is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Including the English text at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we now move to page 273. That's the page you did not have at your disposal. And perhaps this page, do you recognise this page as being your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except that this page is of -- you have some things are in Cyrillic script --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- And some things are in Latin script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But both written --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both written by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please move down so that -- yes. Now, Mr. Re, it seems that in the translation that was given to us on the screen that we jump from page, last three digits, from 259 to 273, and that seems to be the conclusion at this moment. Could you -- perhaps we should take a break and give you an opportunity, unless you have an explanation right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do. It's called selective translation. Whoever translated these or put the request in some years ago, when they looked at it, asked for selective passages to be translated, and this just has not reviewed until the last few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the Defence aware that there presented selected translations with clear references of what pages, because then you would expect the ERN number so and so, it's translated here, and then -- so that it's possible to make a link between the original and the translation? I see everyone nodding no. Mr. Emmerson, you're the first one. Mr. Guy-Smith. And since Mr. Harvey has raised the issue, I take it that he would join this choir of no-nodders.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour will recall that, in fact, these are the very documents that were only disclosed last Wednesday night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they're documents we have been requesting translations of, but when they finally came, there was no explanation that they were anything other than a complete document. In fact, this is the first we've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can say this: From the Prosecution viewpoint, this information -- I didn't speak to the witness myself until shortly before -- several hours before court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was told earlier today that there was selective translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just forgot to tell the Defence. I am going, to an extent, blind, as it may be fairly obvious, through these things. I haven't had a chance to compare the originals with those which I'm taking her to. It's an unfortunate situation. Normally you would spend a long time preparing a witness like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We just haven't been able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can only apologise to my colleagues in the court for this oversight, but there's simply nothing I can do about it at this point. I mean, if the Defence requires an adjournment, I certainly don't oppose it in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way of indicating on the e-court whether something is a translation or selective translation? Because I see on the source attachments, original, and then the ET and a number and then it's translation and the number is the same. Is there any -- I mean, how could possibly the Defence find out in any other way, or is it -- I mean, you would expect that if parts are cut out, that you would find something like a line or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Andjelkovic, first of all, I apologise for you being bothered with a lot of matters which you're not the source of in any way. You said a couple of times that you're a bit tired as well. I suggest that we take a break. I hope that it would help you, and then finish your testimony in-chief after that break. We certainly won't go anywhere beyond 7.00. The Chamber will also consider during the break a few procedural matters, among them this one. I do understand that if you would have thoroughly investigated all of the numbering, that you would have found out that not for all of the original pages there is an English translation page. At the same time, I immediately add to that that if you put a translation on one page, text which originates from two entirely different pages, that the puzzle is not made the easiest one. At least it's good that we have clarified what we have in front of us. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one other difficulty that is created by this, and of course in no way is the witness to blame for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But what follows is that what's been presented by the Prosecution in what we thought was being an orderly date form- and we saw those dates a little while ago, the late April dates, the last of which I think was the 23rd or 24th of April- it now appears to be a chunk of information which this witness received as a human rights monitor, looking into what had happened or what was believed or suspected to have happened to some Serbs in an area where suddenly this word "kidnapped" arises. Are these kidnaps now placed at the end of April or are they at some later stage in the notebook, somewhere in the middle of May? That, of course, is now -- because of these pages being out of order, the whole narrative now becomes suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that chronology is not without relevance and importance for you and that -- I take it that if you'd find perhaps a couple of minutes during the break to see how, together with Mr. Re, or how Mr. Re would, perhaps with your cooperation, assist the Chamber in not being confused any more on these matters. We will adjourn. We'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to the parties that we'll now continue the examination of the witness and that we reserve the last ten minutes, approximately, for some procedural issues, including the information we just received, and try to finish that within ten minutes. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as may become apparent, the Prosecution does have a difficulty at the moment in completing this witness' evidence for the issues which have become apparent during the last hour or so, and I don't think that I could do justice to the Prosecution's case as it concerns this witness if I -- if the case -- if the witness continues and is completed in-chief tonight. In that respect, I regretfully would have to seek an adjournment of the witness' evidence in-chief to allow us to resolve the issue with the diaries and the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- and maybe to complete it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first then ask you the following question: Again, you are the innocent victim of what happens here, that is, procedure; I really feel sorry for you. Mr. Re, does that mean that -- I take it that in preparing the examination-in-chief, that you had all relevant pages you wanted to touch upon, ready in both languages, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. Frankly, no. That's the difficulty. The difficulty is I am faced with a difficulty in -- because of the calling the witnesses in the order and in a compressed manner and having to move them around, we have not been able to prepare this witness and the one who was proposed to be number 1 in the way in which we should have been able to prepare if we were properly to do justice as the case as pleaded. We have found this difficulty with crime base witnesses who are -- we have one here who's ready to testify tomorrow morning and another one who will be here tomorrow night, ready to testify the next day. With this particular type of witness, we have a much greater difficulty because we're trying to cover general material. And it appears, as I found out a little earlier today, that selective translations were made, and I just have not had a chance to compare the original with the -- the original -- the Serbian original with what we had selected and what has gone into e-court. I was not aware of that until earlier. I can't -- as I've said last week, our systems are very much imperfect. There is very little I can do about it at ten past 6.00 tonight to rectify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're saying you have got no table on the English pages to give at least an opportunity to, if need be, to consult the B/C/S pages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, we were able to find them, but it took us quite a lot of effort to find the one page. What would then your suggestion be? When do you think you could overcome these difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it -- I don't know. It requires us to go back and to examine the diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but let me be very practical. Of course I do understand that it takes you a while. Is it your suggestion that we would now interrupt the examination-in-chief of this witness to tell her that we could not continue within a couple of days, and therefore that she would be free to go home and ask her to come back when you are fully prepared? Is that your suggestion? I mean, I see that later on we would have problems with cross-examination anyhow. It's not a matter of one or two days, from what I feel at this moment. Is that a correct presumption, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two observations, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I was asking Mr. Re what his suggestions were, and then I said if you say that fits in well where we are at this moment. I will allow you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would be happy to cross-examine tomorrow on the basis of the passages that the Prosecution have chosen to put in as relevant passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Re, I now return to you. Would it be your suggestion that we -- with, of course, full apologies then for this witness, to ask her to come back at a later stage. Of course, we first have to find out whether -- what the Defence's position would be on that, but is that your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't be in a position to do it tomorrow, to adjourn now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the day after tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we could not possibly ask the witness to stay here for ages and -- okay. So the suggestion is that we adjourn, that the witness would return home and would then come back. But before -- and I don't know whether it's appropriate to discuss this in the presence of the witness. Ms. Andjelkovic, we are at this moment, as you may have noticed, facing major problems in, I would say, the logistics of the preparation of your testimony, and I'm not going to repeat it for the fifth time, but you're fully not in any way responsible for what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with the parties how to proceed. They might want to comment on certain matters which I would consider not to be appropriate, you to be present there to hear all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either be pleased or confused or whatever it would be, to resolve. So therefore I suggest that you leave the courtroom for a moment and that we discuss how to proceed, and of course we'll inform you immediately once a decision has been made in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would first like to hear from the Defence how they respond to the suggestion made by the Prosecution. Mr. Emmerson. And, of course, we have taken note of the fact that you say you're ready to cross-examine the witness tomorrow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I put this in its context, because I mentioned earlier on concerns that I have, by and large, about the housekeeping arrangements for this week and the calling of witnesses. Just to recap very briefly. Finally, as a result of specific requests, we got these translations very late last Wednesday night. I indicated then, on Thursday, that we would try to assess their 800 pages of material for relevance, and we managed to reduce it down to the notebook. Since then, resources have been devoted to preparing a detailed admissibility argument and to -- combing through the notebooks for cross-examination material. The Prosecution made their decision to choose these two witnesses first. They then abandoned SST7/28, to call her later on, and this morning apparently Mr. Re knew that these were selective translations and made his choice to continue calling his witness in-chief on the basis of the selective translations as he knew them to be, without notifying either the Trial Chamber or the Defence of the potential problems that that could give rise to, or indeed notifying the Defence that the work that they were doing, which has occupied a very considerable amount of the time since last Wednesday when those notes were received, was for naught, or liable to be for naught, because halfway through, as he must have anticipated, if he's making the application that he now makes, it was an application that he could and should have made before the witness was called. Now, all of that -- I don't wish to be here bashing, if I may say so, the Prosecution. We all know the difficulties under which they labour. But this falls into a pattern. And we're in this position: As a result of the application Mr. Re is now making, he will then propose to shuffle up the witness list, a crime base witness for tomorrow, for whom we do not have proofing notes and whose cross-examination has not been fully prepared and in respect of whom material has not been uploaded onto the datebase because we've all been working on the basis that these very difficult and voluminous witnesses were the first two witnesses to deal with. And so the situation we find ourselves is -- I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how you respond to Mr. Re's application. It is a surprising state of affairs that it should be made in this way at this time, in light of the way he himself has chosen to conduct it up until now, but there it is. What I inevitably have to say to you is that the consequence will be that any witness he calls tomorrow will only be capable of being cross-examined the following day, because we will need to prepare the cross-examination overnight and to upload material onto the database, and we don't even have the proofing notes for the witness. We have half of the proofing notes for this witness but not the other half and not the critical half. So the situation which I am most anxious to avoid is that this type of pattern should now become ossified into a procedure for this trial. That was the reason why I wrote on the 5th of February the proposals for the organised exchange between the parties of material in preparation for viva voce witnesses, and I make it absolutely clear that we would respectfully submit that it is unfair to expect the Defence to cross-examine a witness who they have not had at least two clear days' notice of when it is they're likely to be called to give evidence and the material they need to cross-examine on. Apart from anything else, that would be the position with any preparation of a cross-examination. But with the additional complication of the necessity for 24 hours' notice to upload material onto the e-court system, it's not merely a forensic necessity for counsel; it's a technical necessity for the efficient management of this trial. And so the reality is that whichever way you look at it, the Prosecution has had four witnesses in -- its first four witnesses it proposed to call, Peter Boukaert, Colonel Crosland, SST7/28, and now this witness. The first three have now all been abandoned whilst work was being done to prepare them, and now it's proposed that this one be abandoned mid-flow. It's entirely a matter for Your Honours how to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Any of the other counsel would like to add something to what has been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it's been well put, and I don't see any need to go further at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm not one to flog a dead horse either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, the Chamber will have to decide on whether we'll tell the Defence that as soon as they're ready and as soon as you've finished your examination-in-chief, that they can cross-examine the witness, which is offered by the Defence. That's one option. The other option is the one you suggested. You said that -- and let me try to find the words exactly. Yes. Let me just find your words. Yes. You said that you're faced with a difficulty, and you said: "We have not been able to prepare this witness and the one who was proposed to be number 1 in the way that we should have been able to prepare if we were properly to do justice as the case -- to the case as pleaded." Isn't it true that much of the confusion could have been prevented by you telling us at an early stage -- I mean, we have discussed over the last couple of days that new notebooks would come in, new material would come, which is not translated, and the Defence claims that they are entitled to have full translation of that material in order to prepare. Now, we see here that large portions are not translated. You were aware of that. We spent half an hour on trying to find out exactly what the witness had in her hands, what exactly the problem was, and I said, "Could you respond?" And you said: "Well, selective translation." You could have also jumped up in the very beginning when we started dealing with these issues and say: I can immediately give you an explanation. I failed to inform you; I failed to inform the Defence. So we are finding ourselves in a situation where we'd like to know what you exactly meant by saying: "If we were properly to do justice the case as pleaded." These are great words for what seems to be insufficient preparation. Could you please tell us exactly what happened? Also, keeping in mind the course of the examination-in-chief as it went on until now. Certainly you'll remember that at a certain moment, quite a number of questions of what happened on the 19th of April finally came back to: "This is what everyone said and what we read in the newspaper." So I'm also wondering what we could expect if we have not these kind of problems, because that was just before we faced these problems. But it is an experience you had, the Chamber had, and the Defence had. So, therefore, I'm wondering what exactly you meant when you are talking about properly to do justice to the case as pleaded. I mean, what would happen if we would not follow your suggestion? Not in practical terms, but what would be -- and that's what you suggest. What would be the damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The damage is that the Prosecution would not be able, in the time available, to get out the evidence in the best way for the -- as recorded in the witness' notes. Now, of course, I take on board Your Honour's criticism of my neglecting to mention earlier that there was a selective translation, and I -- the only thing I can say is I just forgot. It may sound strange to you, but with the pressures of getting this together, I just simply forgot. And Ms. Gustafson, as you may have noticed, has been sitting with me as I'm going through this blind, not having a chance to take the witness through it or go through the diaries before, trying to find them for me; and I just completely forgot that it had been mentioned to me earlier in the day that they weren't fully done. I just forgot. Otherwise, I would have jumped up earlier. I mean, it's obvious, I just forgot until suddenly it became obvious, Oh, this is what was going on, it's in the back of my mind. Now, that has to do with a lot of things and the number of things we've been trying to do in getting the trial together. One of the things here is in this particular Prosecution we only have three lawyers at the moment who can come to court and take witnesses; only two of them can effectively do it at the moment, that's me and Mr. Di Fazio. So the entire burden of this case, a war crimes case, has been placed on the shoulders of myself and Mr. Di Fazio in terms of proofing witnesses, preparing them, and getting them to court and going through it. We have staffing problems in the OTP. Now -- I mean, that's of no concern to the Defence. The problems are we do not have enough lawyers on this case who can go to court and present the evidence. That is why I was unprepared. And all I can do is apologise to the Trial Chamber and my colleagues for being unprepared with this particular witness, who I didn't get to speak to until about 11.30 this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's why I'm unprepared, which is why I can't place before the Trial Chamber everything I wish to. Mr. Di Fazio is proofing another witness, the witness who we propose to call tomorrow or the day after. Then I'll have to do the next one, and so on. Hopefully we'll get another lawyer soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, I think you spent most of your words not on the consequences of the decision to be taken by this Chamber but on what caused the present situation. That's exactly one of the issues raised by Mr. Emmerson, who said, Are we going to experience this every day? Well, I'm translating your words. These are two distinct issues. Under-staffing of the OTP is something that would certainly need -- I mean, the consequence of that for this trial would certainly need more attention under those circumstances, but our first decision we have to take is how to proceed with a witness who is now waiting outside this courtroom. And that was my first and, I would say, my primary question to you. In view of the experience we had until now during the examination-in-chief, what exactly would be the damage? And you told us, Well, we couldn't elicit the evidence as we would wish. That's, of course, a very general answer. And this Chamber is not in a position to forecast how important this witness is for your case, what would happen, whether we could say, Let's leave it for the time being as it is, and if there's -- I mean, it's clear and it's on the record now that you are not sufficiently prepared to hear the evidence of the witness, which would not, under all circumstances, bar you from, at a later stage, applying for recalling her, not to revisit the issues dealt with at this moment but because major portions of the evidence not being elicited for the reasons you just told us. I'm not -- I'm not saying that -- in the limited time you have that it would be an attractive option ever to apply for recalling the witness to -- and it would cause all kinds of problems as well. But I'd like to know from the Defence, is that considered -- I'm not saying -- of course, we'd have to hear the reasons. We would be, then, further in the case. We would have to consider what it adds to the evidence already elicited. But if you would consider this to be a fundamentally inappropriate and prohibited route, under all circumstances, for the Prosecution to, at a later stage, apply and say, We'd like to -- with then full information, We'd like to complete, not to change the testimony given until then, but to explore other areas as well which we have not come to at this moment. Would that fundamentally unacceptable for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I hope it doesn't sound as though I'm in any way avoiding Your Honour's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- but with respect, that is an issue which can only really be addressed as and when any application to recall is made. Generally, I would be -- I'm not entirely in favour of having to cross-examine a witness twice, or rather, cross-examining the witness knowing that the Prosecution might not just re-examine but recall in chief later on other material which wasn't available to me at the time. It's not an ideal situation to be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I would never say never. It would obviously be a matter for Your Honours to consider if and when such an application was made. But please don't assume that I would concede such an application, because I most certainly am not suggesting that that is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We're in the situation we're in because a choice was made by the Prosecution as to how to open the evidence in this case. We're in this position because the Prosecution chose not to begin with crime base witnesses, who they say they can prepare and put on the witness stand with no difficulty. I made it very clear to Mr. Re weeks ago that these were difficult witnesses to handle, with complex questions of potential relevance and admissibility and issues concerning the way in which their evidence was to be properly prepared. I suggested to him weeks ago that if they were going to be called first, the sensible thing would be for him to take fresh statements from them in a proper form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber is not -- of course, I do understand that without being informed all the details of advice you have given to Mr. Re, that you raised the issue at an earlier stage. Let's leave it at that and not go into further detail on matters which are not appropriate, perhaps, for the Chamber to hear. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I might. I believe that earlier in these proceedings I indicated I had some concerns just generally about the disclosure practices that were existing. I think it's important to note that the statement of this witness, which was taken in 2002, was included in the supporting materials and the very notebooks that are in question have been in the knowledge of the Prosecutor's Office for some period of time. But above that and beyond that, the situation that we're in right now is: Had Mr. Harvey not stood up with a confusion that existed - I'm thankful for that - had he not stood up, Mr. Re would have completed his examination and we would have been cross-examining tomorrow. That's what would have occurred. So I fail to see yet, based upon the assertions made by Mr. Re and the questions asked by the Chamber, how in fact there would be any detriment to him. I just don't see it at this point in time. I don't think he would have taken a different position than he'd taken before. You asked a question with regard to the issue of recalling a witness, and in that regard I -- once again, I'll join the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson. I wouldn't know until it came up. I find it an extremely unattractive way of proceeding with a trial for many, many reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly clear to me as well, but I'm exploring the whole range of -- Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are times when I think it's a good thing that I stood up and there are times when I think perhaps I should just have shut up and sat down. It looked good at the time and I'm sorry that it's led to this level of confusion. I would like to proceed with this witness, and I think whether or not this witness should be allowed to be recalled at another stage is obviously a matter that would have to be kept under review. But quite frankly, speaking as bluntly as I can, I don't think this witness is ever going to add a great deal to the sum total of this Tribunal's understanding of the importance of this case. But for all that, I would move that we get on with this witness and finish her in an expeditious fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- on the basis of your experience until now, how much time do you think you would need for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On the basis of the evidence that the witness has given so far, not very long. Certainly not much longer than about half an hour, 40 minutes, in my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Assuming that I'm not going to go over old ground, I would figure probably not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If anything, less than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That leaves us with cross-examination to be completed almost in one session.
