One of the other options that might be available to us as well, Mr. Re, is that where we had already in mind that cross-examination would take place tomorrow anyhow -- you say: "I couldn't possibly continue my examination-in-chief at this moment." You feel that you are -- I'm just exploring all possibilities. What about you finishing your examination-in-chief tomorrow in let's say the first 45 minutes. Then you have an additional period of time to prepare for that and to try to find out what crisis management and damage control, and what all these terms mean today, what you could have achieve until tomorrow. Then give the Defence a break of one hour, one hour and a half, perhaps two hours, and give the Defence an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Re responds to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- a question that raises itself in my mind is that certainly in the jurisdictions in which my colleagues and I practice, recognising that's all different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- once a witness has taken the witness stand, it is not normally permitted for the counsel who calls that witness to communicate with the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I certainly would not -- and I think that's the practice in this Tribunal as well. I would say it was merely to give an opportunity to Mr. Re to re-organise his logistics and to find the proper translation pages, not to restart proofing the witness. That's not what I had in mind when I suggested this solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, could you give me your comment on this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would certainly help. It may - it may - get us out of this pickle we've got ourselves in - it may. I'd certainly take Your Honour's guidance on this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's, then ... [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take -- if it would only be one, two, or three minutes to deliberate on the matter, and so everyone is expected to remain in the courtroom. --- Break taken at 6.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the situation and decided that we'll proceed as follows: We'll not continue the examination-in-chief today. Mr. Re, tomorrow you will have an opportunity to complete the examination-in-chief in the first hour of the afternoon session. Then the Chamber will be flexible as to how long the break should be from what we understand, and just assuming that we don't get major surprises in terms of what evidence to expect tomorrow, that the Defence teams would, together, finish their cross-examination in certainly not more than two hours. From what I understand, two hours is too much for one session. Therefore, if, tomorrow, you say, Well, one hour and a half will do, then we could have one more session to start at the time the Defence considered it's prepared. So at most you would have approximately one and a half, two hours, to further prepare, to further consider. If you would like to start earlier, that's a possibility as well. Of course, part of it could be prepared today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid any further confusion, no one should look at the official court calendar, which still says that we're sitting in the morning, but we are sitting in the afternoon, as everyone knows. No, no, no, just to avoid that half of the parties are here at 9.00 instead of a quarter past 2.00. We'll proceed in this way tomorrow. I'd like to have the witness called in the courtroom. We'll later then pay attention in private session to the remaining procedural matter, but I'd first like to inform the witness about our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Andjelkovic. The Chamber has considered all the options and discussed with the parties. We have decided that we'll proceed in the following way: We'll finish for today. Tomorrow, where it was scheduled that you'd be cross-examined by the Defence, we'll first spend another -- certainly not more than one hour, but at least one short session to finish your examination-in-chief. Then we might have a bit of a longer break and then the Defence counsel will have an opportunity to cross-examine you, and we hope to finish your testimony then tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which would avoid that we have to call you back, as the matter stands now. Again, our apologise. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given already or testimony still to be given tomorrow. So refrain from speaking to anyone about that. Then you're excused for the moment. Madam Usher, could you please escort Ms. Andjelkovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the matter that remains is the report we received this afternoon, and I'd like to turn into a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is another matter I wish to raise, not necessarily in private session, but about witness orders. I'm happy to raise it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we first deal with the rather urgent matter in front of us, and that certainly there will remain a couple of minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Re, you announced that you'd like to raise an issue. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's in relation to the order of witnesses which we would propose to call, and I have -- unlike with other matters, I did discuss this with my colleagues from the Defence before court started today at 2.15. Last week, in the Pre-Trial Conference, I alerted the Chamber to some difficulties we were having with witnesses in this first week, the order and the trial preparation, which meant that we might be asking for some flexibility or some forebearance from the Trial Chamber at least in the first week in terms of the order of witnesses and possibly having to switch them or move to other ones. The situation arose earlier this week when I -- Monday, I think I notified you about - maybe it was Friday; I can't remember now - the proposed first and second witness, asking to switch them. As a result of further speaking to the first witness who was on our list - that's witness 28 - we don't feel we're in a position to call her this week. We would propose, if it's acceptable to the Chamber, to call her at a later stage, several weeks on into the trial, which would give both us and the Defence greater time, of course taking up Mr. Emmerson's words of wisdom here, to prepare for this particular witness. There is one matter of disclosure, and I spoke to the Defence -- Defence counsel before court today, and that is there are documents relating to an organisation which we were only able to -- we only identified and disclosed to them, I think it was, today which pertained to these witnesses. Again, it's one of these things about the identification of material in our system and getting it to the Defence in a timely manner, allowing fairness to the Defence and the smooth flow of procedures. The result, if we don't call that witness this week, is that we still propose to call the third witness on our list. That witness is here. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that witness 38?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's number 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 38 is ready to have her evidence called in chief. Mr. Di Fazio has finished talking to her. The proofing notes are complete. They were disclosed tonight at 22 past 6.00, I'm told, to the Defence counsel. The Prosecution, of course, is entirely aware, entirely understanding, of the difficulties faced with -- faced in terms of cross-examining witnesses and needing all the information. And we -- if there's any embarrassment or difficulty, we certainly don't oppose the Defence asking for the appropriate necessary period to prepare themselves. However, that brings me to the next point, the crux of that; that is, in terms of replacing the first witness, we have someone who would probably be available on Friday but we wouldn't be able to speak to them until Thursday, realistically, and that's witness 19, who's number 29 on the list. Of course, for Thursday we'd be ready to go with the witness who was number 4 on the list. That witness will be arriving in The Hague tomorrow night, and I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your list and the numbering on the list, I never know what -- I have a list in front of me which says "Newest" which gives the witness that was examined today as the first witness on the list. That's the newest version. Could you tell me where this witness is to be found on this list? I can't take always all the lists with me, the old ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Number 29 on order -- in order is the one we'd propose to call on Friday, if it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's witness 19. Yes, I've located that witness. Yes. I take it that the main issue will be -- I take it that you don't take any steps this evening to get this witness in, but at earliest convenience, tomorrow morning. But the issue is not, I would say, whether this Trial Chamber is very flexible on hearing the testimony of Witness A or B; but it's mainly disclosure and time for preparation of cross-examination. Have you discussed it already with Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have. It was one against ten at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith. If you would allow me. It's 7.00. We have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not going to quibble about what happened earlier with regard to the issue of witnesses. I'll make my position very, very clear and very, very simple. We are not in a position to deal with that particular witness at this time. It is -- he is -- that witness is totally out of order. We have been making preparations in an entirely different fashion. This is creating absolute havoc amongst the Defence preparation, and I very strongly object to the entry of that witness at this time. I really request, in the strongest possible terms that I can, that the Prosecution get their house in order. I have not experienced this kind of disorder in cases before here, and it is very, very difficult to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, I hear strong -- stronger words than usual from the Defence side as far as cooperation is concerned. Anything to be added there, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think, if I may, given the time, if there's anything to be added, I'll add it tomorrow. But I'm sure, Your Honour, without the slightest difficulty of imagination, can foresee what the likely response is going to be with all of these witnesses being material, not being disclosed until the very last minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, and one of the things the Chamber will do is also to see what information we have about witness 19 at this moment. So to be in a better position to assess and understand. Mr. Harvey, anything you'd like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In view of the hour, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Re, we'll not decide on the suggestion at this very moment. That means that this week it's scheduled to finish the testimony of the witness Andjelkovic, that the witness 38 will be called later this week, and that we'll hear the testimony of that witness. And on your other suggestion, the Chamber notes at this moment that there seems to be rather strong opposition, and we'll not hurry into a decision now but in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I didn't make myself clear. The witness I was talking about on Friday would be the -- would be the fourth witness. There is a third witness who is number -- she's not protected, but you never know what people say when they get here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's her number? Number 4 on the list. She's proposed to be called on Thursday. She'll be here tomorrow tonight. I don't propose to proof her because I interviewed her last month, and I don't think she's got anything more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember how many on the list. I always get confused because I always think that you're working from a different list than I am. I'm just working on the basis of the last list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The one I have in front of me says witness order; 28 is the first one; Andjelkovic is the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a list in front of me which have witness order, 1, 2, 3, 4, the second being 38, the fourth being 28. That's the list I've got in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's the one after 38. I apologise. I thought it was the one we'd filed I was looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep matters short. Whatever is still on our programme for this week, witness 19 is not yet, to say it as simple as I can. With apologies to the interpreters, I would like to adjourn, Mr. Re, unless there is something that really could not wait until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom. We'll then adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
